Q: Unity IOS build Game A:

This error usually appears when the Firebase version pinned in the Podfile doesn’t match what the Unity Firebase SDK expects.
In Unity iOS builds it’s generally better not to lock Firebase to a specific version and let CocoaPods resolve compatible dependencies on its own.

I’d recommend updating CocoaPods, removing the fixed Firebase version from the Podfile, deleting Pods and Podfile.lock, and running a clean pod install again. Also make sure all Firebase Unity packages are on the same version and that the iOS deployment target meets Firebase’s minimum requirements.

This kind of mismatch between Unity plugins and CocoaPods specs is pretty common and is usually resolved after a clean reinstall with aligned versions.

Q: How to hide a password send to a web API from Windows logging A:

In essence, it is generally a bad practice to script password authentication simply because you can't trust a script. You need to lay the trust in the hands of a user (account) or an organization.
From a technically view, a SecureString is reasonable safe, but putting a plain-text secret in it or getting a plain-text secret out of it is not. So what is the use of a SecureString? Almost nothing, other than just passing it through from a trusted entity to another trusted entity, like this:

$Credential = Get-Credential
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri $Uri -Credential $Credential #...

Where you might conclude that a SecureString shouldn't be used at all and simply rely on the permissions of the current user (or computer) account:

⚠️ Recommendation

Don't use SecureString for new code. When porting code to .NET Core, consider that the contents of the array are not encrypted in memory. The general approach of dealing with credentials is to avoid them and instead rely on other means to authenticate, such as certificates or Windows authentication.

Anyways, if your company doesn't leave you any other option, you might leverage from the feature that the -body parameter accepts either a (json) string or a hash table (dictionary):

When the input is a POST request and the body is a String, the value to the left of the first equals sign (=) is set as a key in the form data and the remaining text is set as the value. To specify multiple keys, use an IDictionary object, such as a hash table, for the Body.

Meaning : do not use a Json-string but use a HashTable instead (knowing that a HashTable is stringified to "System.Collections.Hashtable" in the output):

$Body = @{
    username          = $Credential.UserName
    password          = $Credential.Password | ConvertFrom-SecureString -AsPlainText
    concurrentSession = $true
} # Don't use: | ConvertTo-Json

Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri $Uri -Body $Body -TimeoutSec 2700 # Don't use: -ContentType "application/json"

Windows log:

Again, this is just a workaround called "Security through obscurity". I can't guaranty that your plain-test password might end up anywhere else once retrieved from something like a SecureString!
